newsitem.title: USA: Florida could retry youth in 1993 tourist murder.
newsitem.headline: Florida could retry youth in 1993 tourist murder.

text.p: The confessed killer of a British tourist could face possible life in prison after an appeals court threw out part of his original plea bargain, a state prosecutor said on Friday.
Aundra Akins, serving 27 years in prison as part of a plea agreement, could be sentenced to life if the state decides to retry him, Leon County state attorney Willie Meggs said.

Akins, now 18, pleaded guilty in January 1995 to killing tourist Gary Colley during a botched robbery at a remote interstate highway rest stop in North Florida, a crime that damaged the state's $38-billion-a-year tourist industry.
Colley was the ninth visitor to be slain in Florida in 12 months.

On Thursday, the First District Court of Appeal in Tallahassee threw out a portion of Akins' original plea, saying his deal with prosecutors was invalid. In essence, the court said Akins had pleaded guilty to a non-existent crime in an effort to get out of the tougher charges. The court sent the case back to the circuit court where the trial took place.
Meggs said it would be "some time" before prosecutors decide whether to retry the case. If they do not, Akins would remain in prison under the 27-year sentence for second-degree murder.
"He's not going anywhere," Meggs said. "We want to take some time to review our options."

Akins was the triggerman in the attack that left Colley, a resident of Yorkshire, England, dead and his companion, Margaret Jagger, wounded. After the killing, Florida's governor posted armed guards at highway rest stops.
Under the plea agreement, Akins testified against accomplice John "Billy Joe" Crumitie, 20, who is serving a life sentence for his part in the crime.

Akins pleaded guilty to lesser charges of second-degree murder and attempted first-degree felony murder, but before he was sentenced the Florida Supreme Court threw out the crime of first-degree felony murder as unconstitutional.

Prosecutors and Akins' defence lawyer agreed to substitute another crime in place of the charge declared invalid by the state high court. In its ruling on Thursday, the appellate court said the state could not change the charge, even if it was agreed to by Akins' attorney.
